content: Your doctor has prescribed oxytocin, a hormone that stimulates contractions of the uterus and smooth muscle tissue. This medication may be administered by injection into a large muscle, such as the buttock or hip, or it may be added to an intravenous fluid that is delivered through a needle or catheter into your vein. Oxytocin is a naturally occurring hormone produced by the hypothalamus and stored in the pituitary gland. It is commonly used to initiate or strengthen labor and to control bleeding after childbirth. In some cases, it may be prescribed for other purposes; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and any potential side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is essential to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of treatment will depend on how your symptoms respond to the medication. Before receiving oxytocin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to oxytocin or any other medications. Additionally, provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, including vitamins and supplements. Notify your doctor if you have a history of premature delivery, herpes infection, eclampsia, cervical cancer, previous uterine surgery, uterine prolapse, breech presentation, placenta previa, or any other abnormal positioning of the fetus or umbilical cord. Before administering oxytocin, carefully inspect the solution. It should appear clear and free of any floating particles. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is crucial to follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. If this occurs, contact your healthcare provider immediately to resume your therapy. If you experience any of the following symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately: chest pain or difficulty breathing, confusion, a rapid or irregular heartbeat, a severe headache, or irritation at the injection site. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store your medication as directed by your healthcare provider. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry location when not in use, and always store medications and supplies out of the reach of children. Your healthcare provider will provide instructions on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. If you are receiving oxytocin through an intravenous catheter or under your skin, it is important to recognize the signs of a catheter-related infection. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you notice any of the following symptoms near the catheter site: tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, or pain. Oxytocin is available under the brand names Pitocin® and Syntocinon®.
